System Architecture Workspace

Agentic Core is the main project I wanted to develop. As the idea grew, its components, connections and control logic became difficult to understand as a whole. I built System Architecture Workspace to visualise that complexity and work on the design while teaching myself solutions architecture.

My Hypothetical Idea takes this further: an assistant would turn a customer brief into an explorable 3D Brain, propose mathematical checks and identify questions that need research. Its reviewed model could guide baseline AWS architectures and give customers a clearer way to examine changes. The workspace demonstrates the modelling experience; customer collaboration and automatic generation are planned capabilities.

Hypothetical Idea

From a business idea to a system people can understand, examine and build.

I began thinking about Hypothetical Idea from a solutions architect's perspective: how could I take a customer's business requirements and explain their idea to an assistant that develops an explorable 3D Brain? The assistant would map the journey from user input to intended output, propose the algorithms and mathematical checks behind it, and identify the nodes that need further investigation.

That reviewed model could then become a structured data source for baseline AWS system architectures. Engineers would receive a starting point with requirements, relationships and reasoning attached. Customers could explore the same model, understand its complexity and propose improvements with a clearer view of their effects.

My hypothesis is that keeping those activities connected could reduce repeated explanation and rework, helping engineers reach quality designs faster while making customers more informed participants. Agentic Core was the main project I wanted to develop. Its connected responsibilities and control logic were difficult to understand as a whole, so I built System Architecture Workspace to visualise the idea and work through its complexity while teaching myself solutions architecture.

01

THE CONNECTED MODEL

Give the idea a structure that survives the handover.

A business brief describes what someone wants to achieve. Architecture adds the responsibilities, interfaces, dependencies and operating conditions needed to pursue it. Hypothetical Idea would keep the relationship between these two descriptions visible, so that a component has a reason to exist and a proposed service can be traced to an actual need.

  1. Understand the brief

    Capture users, outcomes, constraints, data sensitivity, scale and success criteria. Ask about gaps before treating an assumption as a requirement.

  2. Develop the 3D Brain

    Propose components and relationships, with their inputs, outputs, owners and failure paths. Let people explore the full idea or isolate one part.

  3. Examine the logic

    Describe the input-to-output algorithm, define properties to check and attach evidence or research questions to the relevant nodes.

  4. Review a revision

    Agree the requirements, resolve important ambiguities and record which model revision the customer and engineer are accepting.

  5. Prepare the baseline

    Map the reviewed model to candidate AWS services, boundaries and operational choices, retaining the reasoning for engineers to refine.

The 3D Brain would be a visual interface to structured information. A node might represent a user, a capability, a decision or a service. An edge would name the relationship, such as a data transfer, dependency or authorisation. Each would retain stable identifiers, provenance and revision history. The same information could support an accessible text view, a 2D reference diagram and an AWS design.

This connection has a research foundation. NIST research on requirements and functional models describes tracing controlled English requirements to model functions and checking their congruity. Hypothetical Idea would explore a broader customer-facing workflow built around that principle of traceability.

02

MATHEMATICS WITH A PURPOSE

Make the reasoning inspectable from input to output.

The assistant's mathematical work should describe what a proposed system does and the conditions under which a specific property holds. A useful starting representation is:

M = (V, E, R, C)

V contains components; E describes relationships; R records requirements; C expresses constraints and assumptions.

For each input-to-output path, the assistant would propose an algorithm with explicit inputs, state transitions, permitted actions, outputs and failure behaviour. It could then suggest checks for properties such as whether an output is reachable, whether required validation precedes release, or whether an operation remains inside its approved permissions.

Consider a workflow that prepares a customer deliverable. An illustrative release rule is: release only when approval, test evidence and owner acceptance all identify the current candidate revision. If the candidate changes, those earlier records cannot justify the new release. An engineer could inspect the rule, model its transitions and test attempts to reuse stale approval.

The method would follow the question. Graph analysis can expose missing paths. State machines and model checking can examine sequencing and permitted actions. Queueing or probabilistic models can explore capacity and reliability under stated assumptions. An AI-produced argument would become a candidate for checking, with its assumptions and evidence visible.

AWS engineers have documented using formal specification and model checking to address difficult distributed-system design problems. AlphaProof research in Nature also demonstrates AI-supported formal mathematical proof search. These establish useful techniques to investigate; applying them to business architecture requires a precise translation of the problem.

Hypothetical Idea would distinguish a missing requirement, an unresolved engineering decision, a property awaiting verification and a potential mathematical research question. Failure to find a proof does not establish that new mathematics is needed. A research flag would need a specific question, the existing methods considered and specialist review. Proofs would cover their formal claims and assumptions; implementation behaviour would still need testing.

03

FROM MODEL TO AWS BASELINE

Give engineers a more useful place to start.

A baseline would package candidate service choices, data flows, trust boundaries, availability requirements and operational responsibilities. Each decision should explain the requirement it addresses, alternatives considered and questions still open. A versioned source model would make it possible to trace a changed requirement into the affected architecture decisions.

Review would consider the six AWS Well-Architected pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability. The goal is to organise the information engineers need for these trade-offs, including workload assumptions and business priorities.

The intended users include engineers in customer teams, AWS partners and AWS-facing roles. Different specialists would use the same model for different decisions:

Solutions architects and cloud architects

Trace the business outcome into capabilities, compare alternatives and explain design trade-offs to stakeholders.

Platform and infrastructure engineers

Identify shared services, account boundaries, reusable infrastructure patterns and integration dependencies.

DevOps engineers

Plan delivery pipelines, environment configuration, change controls and the path toward reviewed infrastructure as code.

Security and network engineers

Examine identity, permissions, data classification, trust boundaries, connectivity and traffic paths.

Site reliability and operations engineers

Study failure paths, observability, recovery expectations and the services that support critical user journeys.

Application and serverless engineers

Clarify API contracts, event flows, processing responsibilities and integration behaviour.

Data and database engineers

Review data ownership, movement, retention, consistency and storage requirements.

AI, ML and MLOps engineers

Map model inference, data pipelines, evaluation, human review and model lifecycle requirements.

FinOps and cloud cost engineers

Connect workload assumptions and service choices to cost drivers, estimates and optimisation options.

These are proposed uses for the baseline. Engineering judgment remains central: selecting concrete resources, validating configuration, testing implementations and approving deployment are further steps. The potential time saving comes from a better handover and less reconstruction of intent.

04

THE CUSTOMER'S VIEW

Let people explore the consequences of an idea.

Invited customers would enter their own project and move from the overall business outcome into individual capabilities. Selecting a node would explain what it contributes, what it depends on, what information it uses and what could change downstream. Plain-language explanations and focused views would make the model approachable without requiring knowledge of AWS service names.

A customer could propose an improvement, edit a requirement or request that a feature be removed. Before applying a change, the workspace would show affected dependencies, assumptions and checks. The engineer could then review it, preserve the previous revision and prepare an updated baseline.

For example, removing a notification feature might affect customer communications, event handling and an audit requirement. A visible impact preview would support a more informed discussion than deleting a box in isolation. Customers would see both the requested change and the reasons an engineer recommends adjusting it.

My expectation is that clearer participation could improve confidence and satisfaction by reducing surprises. Customer access would need project-specific permissions, revision controls and appropriate data handling. Satisfaction would be measured alongside whether people correctly understand the design and its changes.

05

THE RESEARCH FOUNDATION

Established building blocks. A connected idea to evaluate.

The evidence supports several parts of Hypothetical Idea's proposed workflow. It gives a concrete foundation for building and testing the integrated experience. I have not yet measured Hypothetical Idea's effect on engineering speed, design quality or customer satisfaction; those are the outcomes the evaluation should establish.

Language can be connected to formal checks

Amazon Bedrock Automated Reasoning checks separates the translation of natural language into formal logic from validation against policy rules. Its documentation explains that translation can be wrong even when logical validation is sound. Hypothetical Idea would therefore make the translation, rule scope and unanswered questions reviewable.

Visual models and infrastructure code can stay connected

AWS Infrastructure Composer documents a visual canvas synchronised with CloudFormation and SAM templates. This is a practical precedent for keeping an architecture view linked to structured artifacts. Hypothetical Idea's proposed extension starts earlier, with customer intent and the reasoning behind a design.

AI-assisted architecture handovers are technically plausible

An AWS example using Amazon Bedrock Agents describes generating infrastructure code from architecture diagrams with organisational guidance. It demonstrates an implementation path for part of the workflow. Hypothetical Idea would investigate how a reviewed requirements model could make that handover more traceable.

3D merits task-specific testing

Path Tracing in 2D, 3D, and Physicalized Networks reports a preregistered study with 34 users in which 3D produced fewer path-tracing errors than 2D. That comparison used virtual reality and specific interaction techniques. It motivates testing this browser-based 3D Brain on its own tasks, alongside readable 2D and text views.

Together, these sources support the feasibility of investigating traceable requirements, formal checks, visual exploration and structured architecture output. The next contribution would be to connect them into a coherent workflow and measure the value of that connection.

06

THE WORKING PROTOTYPE

System Architecture Workspace is where I am learning by building.

Agentic Core was the main project that led me to build the workspace. Understanding how its requirements, coordinated responsibilities, human approval and verification fitted together became difficult as the idea grew. I needed a tool to see those relationships and work on the system, so I built System Architecture Workspace to examine components and connections, compare views and refine the design.

Today, the prototype contains interactive reference architecture, AWS architecture and 3D Brain views of recorded models. The Brain demonstrates the exploration experience. Conversational model generation, managed customer collaboration and automatic baseline generation belong to the proposed product development path.

The workspace makes the idea tangible: an engineer and a customer could work from related views of the same model, with explanations close to the components they concern. My focus is developing that relationship carefully as I deepen my understanding of solutions architecture.

07

HOW I WOULD TEST THE HYPOTHESIS

Measure the complete path to a quality result.

I would begin with matched business briefs and compare the proposed workflow with conventional design tools and a simpler AI-assisted process. Independent engineers would assess outputs against the same requirements, without knowing their origin where practical. The comparison should include clarification and correction effort.

Engineering speed and quality

Measure time to an acceptable baseline, missed requirements, significant design issues and review rework. Faster generation matters when the reviewed result also meets the quality bar.

Understanding and change accuracy

Ask customers to explain dependencies and predict the consequences of edits. Compare completion time and errors across 3D, 2D and text views.

Customer experience

Record satisfaction, confidence and whether customers correctly understand what they are approving. Examine which interaction features explain any improvement.

Model and control integrity

Check traceability, unresolved assumptions and revision consistency. Exercise stale approvals and changed candidates to verify the implemented rules.

Hypothetical Idea's direction is clear: help people turn an idea into a system they can understand together, then give engineers a stronger foundation for building it. The prototype is the starting point for making that vision measurable.
